subject: maths
title: Shape of data distributions
summary: Describe data displays as symmetric, positively skewed, negatively skewed or bimodal, spot outliers, clusters and gaps, and link shape to the mean and median.
body:
Two classes can have the same average mark but very different results: in one, almost everyone scored near the middle; in the other, most did well and a few struggled badly. The **shape** of a distribution tells this story. Doctors, sports scientists and economists all look at shape before they trust an average.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can describe the shape of a data display as symmetric, positively skewed, negatively skewed or bimodal, spot outliers, clusters and gaps, and explain how shape affects the mean and median.

## Before you start

You need histograms and stem-and-leaf plots from *Histograms and stem-and-leaf plots* and the mean and median from *Mean, median, mode and range (Year 7)*.

**Warm-up**

1. Find the mean of 3, 5, 10. *(Answer: 18 ÷ 3 = 6)*
2. Find the median of 2, 9, 4, 7, 3. *(Answer: in order 2, 3, 4, 7, 9 — the middle is 4)*

## Think of it like this

### A slide in a playground

Picture the side view of a playground slide: a tall ladder at one end and a long, gentle slope running away to the other. Data often looks like that — a big pile of values in one place and a long thin **tail** stretching out to one side. We name the shape after the direction the tail (the slope) points, not where the ladder is.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a slide has just one high point, but some data sets have two peaks, or none at all.

## Key ideas

### Symmetric distributions

A distribution is **symmetric** if its left half is roughly a mirror image of its right half. Most values are in the middle and they thin out evenly on both sides — like the heights of adults. In a symmetric distribution the **mean and median are about equal**.

![A symmetric histogram of heights from 140 to 200 cm with frequencies 2, 7, 13, 12, 7, 2 — highest in the middle and falling away evenly on both sides](/diagrams/y9/maths/shape-of-data-distributions-sym.svg)

### Skewed distributions

A **skewed** distribution has a long tail on one side.

- **Positively skewed** — the tail points to the right (towards the larger values). Most values are small, with a few large ones. Example: the number of pets people own.
- **Negatively skewed** — the tail points to the left (towards the smaller values). Most values are large, with a few small ones. Example: marks on an easy test.

![A positively skewed histogram of number of pets: frequencies 14, 11, 6, 3, 2, 1, 1 for 0 to 6 pets — tall bars at 0 and 1 pet and a long low tail stretching right to 6](/diagrams/y9/maths/shape-of-data-distributions-pos.svg)

![A negatively skewed histogram of test marks: tall bars from 70 to 100 percent and a long low tail stretching left to 30](/diagrams/y9/maths/shape-of-data-distributions-neg.svg)

The tail pulls the mean towards it, but hardly moves the median. So:

| Shape | Mean compared with median |
|---|---|
| Symmetric | about equal |
| Positively skewed (tail right) | mean greater than median |
| Negatively skewed (tail left) | mean less than median |

### Bimodal distributions

A **bimodal** distribution has two clear peaks. This often means two different groups have been mixed together — for example, the heights of a group of Year 3 students and their parents.

### Outliers, clusters and gaps

- An **outlier** is a value a long way from the rest of the data.
- A **cluster** is a group of values bunched close together.
- A **gap** is an interval with no values in it.

When you describe a display, mention its shape, then any outliers, clusters or gaps.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Describe the shape of the "number of pets" histogram in Key ideas.

Step 1: find where most values are — the tallest bars are at 0 and 1 pet, on the left.
Step 2: find the tail — the bars get lower and lower towards 6 pets, so the long tail points right.
Step 3: name the shape — tail to the right means **positively skewed**.

### Example 2

A dot plot shows how many minutes 16 students took to finish a puzzle:
4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 28.

![A dot plot of 16 puzzle times: one cluster of dots from 4 to 8, a second cluster from 13 to 16, and a single dot at 28](/diagrams/y9/maths/shape-of-data-distributions-ex2.svg)

Describe the distribution.

Step 1: look for groups of dots — there is a **cluster** from 4 to 8 minutes and another from 13 to 16 minutes.
Step 2: look for empty intervals — there is a **gap** between 8 and 13 minutes.
Step 3: look for lonely values — 28 is far from the rest, so it is an **outlier**.
Step 4: two peaks (6 and the 13–16 group) means the distribution is roughly **bimodal**. Perhaps two groups of students (for example, ones who had seen the puzzle before) are mixed together.

### Example 3

Fourteen students recorded how many minutes they spent on homework one night. Ordered stem-and-leaf plot (key 1 | 1 means 11):

| Stem | Leaf |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 8 |
| 2 | 1 3 7 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 4 | 5 |

Describe the shape, then check the mean and median agree with it.

Step 1: shape — most leaves are on stem 1, and the rows get shorter going down to 45, so the tail points to the larger values: **positively skewed**.
Step 2: mean — the total is 275, so the mean = 275 ÷ 14 ≈ **19.6** minutes.
Step 3: median — 14 values, so average the 7th and 8th: (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = **15.5** minutes.
Step 4: check — mean (19.6) is greater than median (15.5) ✓, just as a positive skew predicts. The few long homework times pull the mean up.

## Common mistakes

- **Naming the skew after the peak instead of the tail.** A peak on the left with a tail to the right is POSITIVELY skewed. Fix: follow the tail.
- **Calling any uneven display "skewed".** Two peaks is bimodal, not skewed. Fix: count the peaks first.
- **Calling the lowest or highest value an outlier automatically.** An outlier must be far from the rest, not just the end of the data.
- **Thinking the median moves with the tail.** The tail mostly drags the mean; the median hardly changes.

## Tips to remember

- **"The tail tells the tale"** (made-up memory trick): the side the long tail points to names the skew.
- **Positive = pointing to the positive (bigger) end of the number line; negative = pointing to the smaller end.**
- **Mean follows the tail like a dog on a lead** (made-up): tail right → mean bigger than median; tail left → mean smaller.
- **Two humps, two groups:** a bimodal shape is a clue that two different groups are mixed together.
- **Describe in this order — S, O, C, G:** shape, outliers, clusters, gaps.

## Key terms

- **Distribution** — the way the values of a data set are spread out.
- **Symmetric** — a distribution whose two halves are roughly mirror images.
- **Positively skewed** — a distribution with a long tail towards the larger values (to the right).
- **Negatively skewed** — a distribution with a long tail towards the smaller values (to the left).
- **Bimodal** — a distribution with two clear peaks.
- **Outlier** — a value far away from the rest of the data.
- **Cluster** — a group of values bunched close together.
- **Gap** — an interval of the scale where there are no values.

## Summary

- Shape is described as symmetric, positively skewed, negatively skewed or bimodal.
- Name a skew by the direction of its long tail: right is positive, left is negative.
- The tail pulls the mean towards it: positive skew gives mean greater than median, negative skew gives mean less than median.
- Also describe outliers, clusters and gaps.
- Two peaks often mean two different groups are mixed together.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows how many goals were scored in each of 40 netball quarters. Which word best describes the shape of the distribution?
questions.explanation: The peak is on the left and the long tail points right, towards larger values, so it is positively skewed. Naming the skew after the peak (left) gives "negative" by mistake.
steps: Find the peak: the tallest bars are on the left, at low numbers of goals.
Find the tail: the bars fall away slowly to the right.
Tail to the right = positively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the long tail points to the right (the larger values). A tail to the right is positive.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the two sides are not mirror images — one side has a long low tail.
mistakes.D: Step 1: there is only one peak, on the left. Bimodal needs two clear peaks.

questions.prompt: The dot plot shows how many text messages 11 friends sent in one hour. Which value is an outlier?
questions.explanation: 19 is far away from the main group (3 to 8), so it is an outlier. 3 is the smallest value but it is still close to the others.
steps: The main group of dots is from 3 to 8.
An outlier is a value far from the rest: only 19 sits on its own.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 3 is the smallest value, but it sits right next to the other dots. An outlier is far from the rest.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 5 is the most common value (the mode), in the middle of the group — not far from the others.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 8 is the end of the main group, close to 7. Look for the dot that sits on its own.

questions.diagram_alt: A dot plot of texts sent: dots at 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8 and one dot on its own at 19

questions.prompt: A distribution has most of its values at the high end and a long tail stretching towards the low values. What is it called?
questions.explanation: A long tail towards the smaller values (the left) is negatively skewed. Calling it positive names it after where most values are, instead of the tail.
steps: The skew is named after the direction of the long tail.
The tail points to the low (left) end, so it is negatively skewed.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the skew is named after the TAIL, not the peak. A tail towards the low values is negative.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a long tail on one side means the halves are not mirror images.
mistakes.D: Step 1: nothing says there are two peaks. One pile and one tail is a skew.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the ages of 60 people at a school music concert. Which word best describes the shape?
questions.explanation: There are two clear peaks (around 10–15 and 40–45 years) with a dip between, so it is bimodal — probably students and their parents. It is not "symmetric": the key feature is the two peaks.
steps: Count the peaks: one around 10–15 years and one around 40–45 years.
Two clear peaks = bimodal (two groups: students and parents).

mistakes.A: Step 1: the halves look roughly similar, but there are two separate peaks with a dip between them. Count the peaks first.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a skew has one peak and a long tail. This display has two peaks.
mistakes.D: Step 1: a skew has one peak and a long tail. This display has two peaks.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of ages of 60 people from 5 to 50 years in classes of width 5, with frequencies 9, 14, 5, 2, 1, 4, 10, 12 and 3 — two peaks

questions.prompt: A Year 9 maths quiz was very easy: nearly everyone scored 8, 9 or 10 out of 10, and just a few students scored low. What shape would a histogram of the scores most likely have?
questions.explanation: The pile is at the high scores and the few low scores form a tail to the left, so the shape is negatively skewed. "Positive" mixes up the tail with the pile.
steps: Most values are high (8 to 10), so the peak is on the right.
The few low scores make a long tail to the left: negatively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the few LOW scores make the tail, and low is on the left. A tail to the left is negative.
mistakes.B: Step 1: most scores are piled up at the top end, not in the middle, so it cannot be a mirror image.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there is one big pile (8 to 10), not two separate peaks.

questions.prompt: The dot plot shows the number of push-ups 14 students did in one minute. Which statement is true?

options.A: There are two clusters, with a gap between 5 and 12
options.B: There is one cluster from 2 to 15 with no gaps

questions.explanation: There is one group from 2 to 5, an empty stretch from 6 to 11, and a second group from 12 to 15: two clusters and a gap. 15 is not an outlier because it belongs to the second group.
steps: Find groups: one from 2 to 5 and another from 12 to 15 — two clusters.
Find empty stretches: nobody did 6 to 11 push-ups — a gap between 5 and 12.
No single dot is far from everything, so there is no outlier.

mistakes.B: Step 2: no student did 6 to 11 push-ups, so there is an empty stretch. Look for intervals with no dots.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 15 sits right next to 14 in the second group. An outlier is far from ALL the other values.
mistakes.D: Step 1: there is no single peak with a long tail — there are two separate groups.

questions.diagram_alt: A dot plot of push-ups: dots at 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, then nothing from 6 to 11, then dots at 12, 13, 13, 14, 14 and 15

options.A: Negatively skewed; the mean (5.5) is greater than the median (4)
options.B: Symmetric; the mean equals the median
options.C: Positively skewed; the mean (5.5) is greater than the median (4)
options.D: Positively skewed; the mean (4) is less than the median (5.5)

questions.explanation: The tail (9, 15) is at the high end, so it is positively skewed; the mean is 55 ÷ 10 = 5.5 and the median is (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4, so the mean is bigger, as positive skew predicts. Calling it negative names the shape after the pile.
steps: Shape: most values are 2 to 6 and a tail stretches up to 15, so it is positively skewed.
Median = average of the 5th and 6th values = (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4, so the mean is greater than the median.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the long tail (9 and 15) is at the large end, which is positive skew.
mistakes.B: Step 2: work out both. The total is 55, so the mean is 5.5, but the median is 4 — they are not equal.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the values are swapped. The mean is total ÷ count; the median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: The parallel dot plots show the hours of sport played in a week by 9 students in Club A and 9 students in Club B. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Club A is roughly symmetric; Club B is negatively skewed
options.B: Club A is roughly symmetric; Club B is positively skewed
options.D: Club A is bimodal; Club B is symmetric

questions.explanation: Club A peaks at 7 and falls away evenly, so it is symmetric; Club B piles up at 3–4 with a tail to 11, so it is positively skewed. "Negatively skewed" names Club B after its pile rather than its tail.
steps: Club A: the dots peak at 7 and fall away evenly on both sides — roughly symmetric.
Club B: most dots are at 3 and 4, with a tail stretching right to 11 — positively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: Club B’s long tail stretches towards the larger values (8 and 11), so its skew is positive.
mistakes.C: Step 1: Club A’s dots rise to a peak at 7 and fall away evenly on both sides — that is symmetric.
mistakes.D: Step 1: Club A has only one peak, at 7. Club B is piled at the left with a tail to the right.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of hours of sport. Club A: 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9. Club B: 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 11

questions.prompt:
Ordered stem-and-leaf plot of the number of laps 23 swimmers completed (key 2 | 4 means 24):
1 | 8 9
2 | 2 4 5 6 7 8
3 | 0 1 3 4 5 7 9
4 | 1 2 5 6 8
5 | 0 3
6 |
7 |
8 | 6
Which description is best?

options.A: Roughly symmetric, with an outlier at 86
options.C: Negatively skewed, with an outlier at 18
options.D: Bimodal, with a gap from 50 to 60

questions.explanation: Ignoring 86, the rows have 2, 6, 7, 5 and 2 leaves — rising to one peak and falling evenly — so the shape is roughly symmetric. The empty stems 6 and 7 show 86 is far from the rest: an outlier.
steps: Ignore the lonely value first: the rows for stems 1 to 5 have 2, 6, 7, 5, 2 leaves — one peak in the middle, roughly symmetric.
Stems 6 and 7 are empty, so 86 is far from all other values.
Best description: roughly symmetric, with an outlier at 86.

mistakes.B: Step 2: one value (86) on its own does not make a tail — it is far from everything else, so it is an outlier.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 18 is right next to 19 and 22, so it is not an outlier. Look for the value separated by empty rows.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the rows rise to one peak (stem 3) and fall again — there is only one peak.

questions.prompt: Data: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 52. The outlier 52 is removed. How do the mean and median change?

options.B: The mean falls by 0.5; the median falls by about 4.6
options.C: The mean falls by 6.5; the median does not change
options.D: The mean falls by about 4.6; the median falls by 0.5

questions.explanation: Before: mean 159 ÷ 8 = 19.875, median (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5. After: mean 107 ÷ 7 ≈ 15.29, median 15. The mean drops about 4.6 but the median only 0.5 — the outlier mostly affects the mean.
steps: After removing 52: total 107, mean = 107 ÷ 7 ≈ 15.29.
New median = 4th of 7 values = 15. So the mean falls by about 4.6 and the median by 0.5.

mistakes.A: Step 3: work out the new median separately. With 7 values it is the 4th value, 15 — only 0.5 lower than 15.5.
mistakes.B: Step 3: these are swapped. An outlier pulls the mean a lot and the median only a little.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the new mean is 107 ÷ 7, not 52 ÷ 8 less than the old mean. And the median moves, because the number of values changes.

questions.prompt: Which of these data sets is the histogram most likely to show? (The horizontal axis is 0 to 100.)

options.A: Number of goals scored per game by a soccer team
options.C: Percentage marks on a very easy test
options.D: Ages of everyone at a primary school assembly (students and teachers)

questions.explanation: The histogram is piled up at the high values with a long tail to the left (negatively skewed) — like an easy test where most students score highly. Goals per game would be skewed the other way.
steps: Describe the shape: most values are high (70 to 100) and a tail stretches left — negatively skewed.
Ask which context has mostly high values and a few low ones: marks on a very easy test.

mistakes.A: Step 2: goals per game are mostly small numbers with a few big ones — a tail to the RIGHT. This histogram’s tail is on the left.
mistakes.B: Step 1: adult heights are roughly symmetric. This histogram is piled at the high end with a tail to the left.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that would be mostly young children plus a few adults, with two groups — a pile on the left, not the right.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram with values from 0 to 100 in classes of width 10 and frequencies 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 15 and 9 — piled at the high end with a long tail to the left

questions.prompt: A coach recorded the 100 m swim times (seconds) of a junior squad and a senior squad and combined them into the dot plot shown. Why is the combined distribution bimodal?

options.A: Some times must have been recorded wrongly
options.B: Two groups with different typical times have been mixed together

questions.explanation: One cluster (around 13 s) and a second cluster (around 18 s) appear because two groups with different typical times are combined. It is not a skew, which would have only one peak.
steps: The dot plot has two peaks, around 13 s and around 18 s — bimodal.
Two peaks usually mean two different groups are mixed: here the two squads have different typical times.

mistakes.A: Step 2: two peaks do not mean errors. Think about who was timed — two different groups.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a skewed shape has one peak and a long tail. This plot has two separate peaks.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that would double the dots but not split them into two groups. Look at how the two squads differ.

questions.diagram_alt: A dot plot of 18 swim times from 11 to 20 seconds with two humps: one peaking at 13 seconds (values 11 to 15) and one peaking at 18 seconds (values 16 to 20)
